scenes.title: Ask BC — inside the BigCommerce control panel
scenes.caption: So this is Ask BC, and the important thing is where it lives — inside the BigCommerce admin, not a separate app. That matters because the merchant doesn't context-switch. They're already here managing orders and products. The green dot is a live WebSocket to a Cloudflare Worker — not an API route, not a polling loop, a persistent connection to a Durable Object that holds this merchant's session state.

scenes.title: One question, six metrics
scenes.caption: I asked for a store summary. What came back isn't markdown — those are real React components rendered inline. Functionally, the merchant got their answer in six seconds instead of clicking through four different admin pages. Technically, the agent wrote one TypeScript script that called four APIs in parallel and computed derived metrics in memory. That's the Codemode advantage — one execution replaces what would've been ten serial tool calls on a traditional agent.

scenes.title: Structured tables with follow-up suggestions
scenes.caption: Products table with real SKUs. But the 'so what' is below it — follow-up suggestions generated from the response content. The merchant doesn't have to figure out what to ask next. That's the difference between a chatbot and an assistant — an assistant anticipates the next question. Copy and feedback buttons on every response, because the merchant owns this data and might need it in a spreadsheet or a Slack message.

scenes.title: Three-way join — orders, line items, customers
scenes.caption: This is the query that breaks traditional agent architectures. Five orders with per-line-item detail from three different API surfaces, joined in memory, with computed totals. On a tool-calling agent, this would chain seven or eight serial round-trips and likely hit a step limit before finishing. With Codemode, the model writes one script that fetches everything in parallel and returns structured tables. Architecturally, that's the argument for code generation over tool calling — the model plans the entire query graph upfront instead of discovering it one call at a time.

scenes.title: Transparent tool usage
scenes.caption: Every response shows which tools the agent called. This matters for trust — when an AI tells a merchant their revenue is eighty-one thousand dollars, the merchant needs to know where that number came from. Expand the indicator, see the exact APIs. It's also a debugging surface for us — if the agent gives a wrong answer, we can trace which tools it called and what data it saw.

scenes.title: Write operations — preview before execution
scenes.caption: Now the agent isn't just reading — it's about to change the store. I said 'create a coupon,' and it did something important: it previewed the operation first. Showed me the exact arguments — code, discount type, amount — and asked to confirm. Functionally, the merchant stays in control. Technically, write tools use a two-turn pattern — the first call returns a preview, the second call with confirmation actually executes. The store doesn't change until the merchant explicitly says yes.

scenes.title: Confirmed and created
scenes.caption: I confirmed, and coupon REEL twenty-five is now live in BigCommerce. Coupon ID four, twenty-five percent off, store-wide. That's not a mock — I can go verify it in the marketing section right now. Architecturally, write tools live outside the Codemode sandbox — the model can't accidentally trigger a write from inside generated code. Every mutation flows through an explicit tool call with typed arguments and an audit log in the Durable Object's SQLite.

scenes.title: How-to questions
scenes.caption: And it's not just data. I asked how to set up free shipping, and instead of a generic answer, it gave three concrete options with specific navigation paths in the admin. Then offered to create the coupon right there in the chat. That's the 'so what' for the merchant — one surface for 'what is my store doing' and 'how do I make my store do something different.' They don't need to search help docs and then come back to the admin to act on what they learned.

scenes.title: Why Codemode
scenes.caption: Here's the architectural core. The model writes TypeScript, not tool calls. That code runs in a Dynamic Worker sandbox with zero network access. The only way out is typed RPC functions that resolve back to the host worker — which holds the merchant's BigCommerce access token. The token never appears in generated code. This is the same credential isolation architecture Cloudflare uses in Agent Lee. Promise-dot-all for parallelism, in-memory joins, defensive error handling — the model writes the kind of code a developer would.

scenes.title: The architecture
scenes.caption: Two services, clear responsibilities. Vercel handles what it's good at — OAuth, server-rendered pages, the iframe shell, React components. Cloudflare handles what it's good at — long-lived WebSocket connections, per-tenant Durable Objects, sub-ten-millisecond sandbox execution. Credentials are encrypted at rest in Upstash Redis and resolved per merchant at runtime. The 'so what' architecturally — no single-tenant shortcuts. Every piece of this scales to a thousand stores without code changes.

scenes.title: Twenty-nine curated tools
scenes.caption: Twenty-nine tools generated from BigCommerce's own OpenAPI specs. Not hand-waved descriptions — real typed interfaces the model writes code against. Twenty-two reads inside the sandbox. Seven writes outside it with two-turn confirmation. The curation matters — we taught the model that V2 orders return bare arrays with string-typed numbers, that status ID ten means completed, that the coupons endpoint requires an applies-to field. That domain knowledge is what makes the agent work on the first try instead of burning retries discovering API quirks.

scenes.title: Your store, operating itself
scenes.caption: That's Ask BC. The 'so what' for the merchant — they don't learn a new tool, they just talk to the one they already have. The 'so what' for the platform — every BigCommerce store gets an AI operator that reads, writes, and explains, from a single marketplace install. The 'so what' for anyone building this — Codemode plus curated tools plus generative UI is the pattern. It works.
